query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled high‐temperature oxidation treatment that forms a self-renewing, conformal oxide layer on a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will lower the coefficient of friction and wear rate relative to the untreated alloy over the full range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix with no surface modification.
generation.intervention: Apply a precise oxidation treatment (e.g., reactive ion-assisted oxidation or controlled furnace oxidation) to create a thin, ductile, adherent oxide layer on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted over a temperature range of ~25 °C to 800 °C, under both low and high normal loads, in air and in inert environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A conformal, self-renewing oxide layer that acts as a solid lubricant and protective barrier.
generation.mechanism: Frictional heating and environmental oxygen promote the in situ formation and regeneration of a lubricious oxide film that minimizes direct metal–metal contact. This film reduces adhesion and plastic deformation at the contact interface, leading to lower shear strength and improved wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The oxidized surface will exhibit a lower and more stable friction coefficient and a reduced specific wear rate compared to the untreated CoCrFeNi alloy, across the specified temperature, load, and environmental boundaries.
generation.baseline: Untreated CoCrFeNi alloy which shows higher friction and wear due to adhesive and oxidative wear mechanisms, especially at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective for sliding contacts between ~25 °C to 800 °C, under moderate to high loads in both oxygen-rich (air) and inert conditions; performance outside these parameters or under rapid thermal cycling remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The precise stability, thickness, and self-healing capability of the oxide layer under dynamic sliding conditions and variable environmental factors are not fully characterized, and the long-term durability under cyclic extreme conditions warrants further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct pin-on-disk sliding experiments using both untreated and oxidized CoCrFeNi samples. The test should cycle the temperature from room temperature to 800 °C under defined low and high normal loads in both ambient air and an inert atmosphere. Pre- and post-test surface analyses will also be performed to assess oxide layer integrity.
measurements: Surface oxide layer thickness and morphology (using microscopy/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidized samples do not consistently demonstrate a lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate compared to the untreated samples across the full temperature range and varied loads, or if the oxide layer is found to degrade rapidly under sliding conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

decision.trend: Early work on high-entropy alloys (HEAs) such as CoCrFeMnNi revealed that refining grain structure or inducing dynamic amorphization can lower friction in controlled environs (PMC7311485). Attempts to strengthen or toughen CoCrFeNi-type alloys through element additions (e.g. W in AlCoCrFeNiWx) improved high-temperature wear resistance (PMC8470387) but did not systematically resolve friction stability over broad temperature ranges. Multi-principal element alloys with nanohierarchical architectures (PMC10241162) and novel self-lubricating high-entropy materials (PMC12019924) have achieved remarkable wear resistance from room temperature to ~800 °C in model alloys. However, these studies have not fully clarified how to maintain persistently low friction and wear specifically in CoCrFeNi matrices across varying loads and environments, nor have they established robust solutions that avoid extensive compositional modifications.
decision.unsolved: While some high-entropy or complex concentrated alloys exhibit promising friction and wear behavior, there remains limited understanding of how to stabilize low friction and wear in CoCrFeNi across the entire 25–800 °C range under fluctuating loads and environmental conditions. Strategies like alloying additions and exotic second-phase formation achieve partial success but do not fully close the gap on ensuring robust, broad-temperature tribological performance for CoCrFeNi materials.
decision.lever: Implement a high-temperature oxide-forming surface modification that produces a conformal, ductile oxide layer under sliding contact. For example, a controlled oxidation treatment or reactive ion-assisted deposition that fosters a wear-protective, self-renewing oxide film at the contact interface. Once sliding begins, frictional heat and environment-driven reactions form a stable tribo-oxide possessing low shear strength and strong adhesion to the substrate, preventing metal–metal contact from ambient temperatures to ~800 °C.
decision.why: This follows from prior findings that show (1) dynamic near-surface restructuring and oxide film formation can substantially reduce friction in high-entropy alloys (PMC7311485), (2) enhanced wear resistance at elevated temperatures often hinges on robust surface layers (PMC8470387), and (3) carefully engineered, stable tribo-layers can protect wide-temperature tribological performance in related multi-principal element alloys (PMC10241162, PMC12019924). A controlled lab-scale pin-on-disk test, cycling from ambient to 800 °C in both air and inert environments while measuring friction and wear continuously, would reveal if friction remains below the baseline CoCrFeNi coefficient and if wear remains suppressed. Should friction or wear degrade relative to the unmodified alloy, it would falsify the hypothesis.
